decks.module: Stopping, passing and following large vehicles
decks.domain: Large vehicle, emergency and traffic stop confusables

cards.front: Why do large vehicles take longer to stop than cars?
cards.back: Because of their size and weight, large vehicles take longer to stop than cars.

cards.front: How far does a loaded truck need to stop at highway speed in ideal conditions?
cards.back: A loaded truck with good tires and properly adjusted brakes, in ideal conditions at fifty-five miles per hour, needs at least three hundred thirty-five feet to stop, more than one and a half times a car's stopping distance.

cards.front: How do a truck's front and rear no zones differ?
cards.back: The front no zone is about the truck's long stopping distance of at least three hundred thirty-five feet when loaded at fifty-five miles per hour, while the rear no zone is a blind spot reaching up to two hundred feet behind it.

cards.front: Why should you never change lanes or pull out in front of a large vehicle?
cards.back: Because trucks stop so slowly, never pull onto a road or change lanes in front of a large vehicle.

cards.front: When is it safe to move back in front of a truck you passed?
cards.back: When passing a large vehicle, wait until its whole front shows in your rearview mirror before moving in front of it, and keep up your speed.

cards.front: What blind spot do large vehicles have that cars lack?
cards.back: Unlike cars, large vehicles have huge blind spots directly behind them that reach up to two hundred feet.

cards.front: What goes wrong when you follow a large vehicle too closely?
cards.back: Following too close behind a large vehicle leaves you unseen by its driver, unable to see ahead, and with nowhere to go if it brakes suddenly.

cards.front: Where should you position your vehicle behind a large vehicle?
cards.back: Do not follow a large vehicle too closely, and position your vehicle so its driver can see you in the side mirrors.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: large vehicle no zones and turns, emergency vehicles, law enforcement stops, the move-over law and slow-moving vehicles

cards.front: Why do large vehicles use the right lane on steep hills?
cards.back: On steep hills, up or down, large vehicles must travel slowly, about thirty-five miles per hour, and so they use the right lane.

cards.front: Where should you stay out of the right lane when possible?
cards.back: Where possible, stay out of the right lane on hills and near truck weigh stations, where trucks try to re-enter faster traffic.

cards.front: How do hills and weigh stations each make the right lane risky?
cards.back: Trucks crawl in the right lane on steep hills, while near weigh stations the right lane is where trucks merge back into faster traffic; both are reasons to stay out of that lane.

cards.front: What should you watch for and give a maneuvering large vehicle?
cards.back: Pay close attention to a large vehicle's turn signals and give it plenty of room to maneuver.

cards.front: Why might a truck swing left before turning right?
cards.back: To turn right, a truck or bus driver may first swing wide to the left, sometimes using space from other lanes, to clear the curb corner.

cards.front: What should you never do while a truck or bus turns right?
cards.back: Never try to slip between a turning truck or bus and the curb, where you could be squeezed into a serious collision; wait until it has finished its turn.

cards.front: How should you position yourself when meeting an oncoming truck?
cards.back: When meeting a truck from the opposite direction, keep as far right as you can to avoid a sideswipe and to reduce the wind turbulence that pushes the two vehicles apart.

cards.front: What should you do if unsure of an approaching truck's speed before turning left?
cards.back: Many large-vehicle collisions happen at intersections when drivers misjudge an approaching truck's speed before turning left, so if in doubt, do not turn left in its path.

cards.front: Why should you always stop behind the stop line?
cards.back: Stop lines set you farther back at an intersection so larger vehicles have more room to turn, so always stop behind them.

cards.front: Is it worth cutting off a truck to make your exit?
cards.back: Never cut off a large vehicle, whether to make your exit or turn or to get ahead of a truck before a single-lane construction zone, because saving a few seconds is not worth a life.

decks.module: Emergency vehicles and the move-over law
decks.domain: Large vehicle, emergency and traffic stop confusables

cards.front: Why do emergency vehicles use sirens, flashing lights and special horns?
cards.back: Emergency vehicles carry sirens, flashing lights and special horns to help them move through traffic more efficiently.

cards.front: How do you yield to an emergency vehicle with lights and siren on?
cards.back: When an emergency vehicle has its flashing lights and siren on, yield by pulling over to the edge of the road so it can pass, and try not to block intersections, roads or driveways.

cards.front: How does yielding to a moving emergency vehicle differ from a stopped one?
cards.back: For a moving emergency vehicle with lights and siren on, you pull over to the road's edge, which differs from the lane change or slowdown used for a stopped one.
cards.memory_hook: Moving: pull over. Stopped: move over

cards.front: What does South Carolina's move-over law require?
cards.back: Because more and more responders and tow truck operators are being struck on the road, South Carolina has a move-over law requiring drivers to slow down and change lanes when approaching emergency vehicles.

cards.front: What should you do when approaching a stopped emergency vehicle?
cards.back: When approaching a stopped authorized emergency vehicle, proceed with caution, slow down and yield by changing into a lane away from it if safety and traffic allow.

cards.front: What if changing lanes away from a stopped emergency vehicle is unsafe?
cards.back: If changing lanes away from a stopped emergency vehicle is unsafe, slow down and continue with caution at a speed that is safe for traffic conditions.

decks.domain: Large vehicle, emergency and traffic stop confusables

cards.front: Why might an officer make a traffic stop?
cards.back: An officer makes a traffic stop after seeing a traffic violation or while conducting a police investigation.

cards.front: What should you do when you see emergency lights behind you?
cards.back: When you see emergency lights behind you, stay calm, turn on your signal and pull to the side of the road as soon as you safely can.

cards.front: What should you do once you have stopped for an officer?
cards.back: Once stopped, turn off the ignition and radio, switch on your hazard flashers and stay in your vehicle unless the officer tells you to get out.

cards.front: What should you do at night after an officer stops you?
cards.back: At night an officer may shine a spotlight on your vehicle, so switch on the interior lights right after stopping, which lets the officer see into the vehicle.

cards.front: Where should your hands be during a traffic stop?
cards.back: Keep your hands on the steering wheel where they are easy to see, and have passengers stay calm, stay belted in the vehicle and keep their hands in plain view.

cards.front: What should you avoid doing before the officer gives instructions?
cards.back: Neither you nor your passengers should use phones or other devices, and do not make sudden movements or dig for your license or papers before the officer gives instructions.

cards.front: When should you tell the officer about weapons in the vehicle?
cards.back: If there are any weapons in the vehicle, tell the officer about all of them at first contact, and concealed weapons permit holders should follow their CWP procedures.

cards.front: What can you ask an officer in an unmarked car or without a uniform?
cards.back: Roll down your window to talk with the officer, and if the officer is in an unmarked vehicle or not in uniform, ask to see law enforcement credentials.

cards.front: What should you do if your documents are out of reach?
cards.back: The officer may ask for your driver's license, proof of insurance and vehicle registration, and if they are out of reach, say where they are and ask before reaching for them.

cards.front: What should you do if the officer asks you to step out?
cards.back: If the officer asks you to step out, stay safely away from traffic and keep your hands in plain view.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: large vehicle no zones and turns, emergency vehicles, law enforcement stops, the move-over law and slow-moving vehicles

cards.front: What should you do if you disagree with a ticket?
cards.back: The officer may issue a warning or a traffic ticket that may include a fine, and if you disagree, do not argue at the roadside, because you can explain your side in court.

cards.front: Does accepting a traffic ticket admit guilt?
cards.back: Accepting a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt.

cards.front: Where do you contest a ticket you accepted?
cards.back: Accepting a ticket does not mean you admit guilt, and contesting it happens in court rather than by arguing with the officer.

cards.front: Must you sign a traffic ticket in South Carolina?
cards.back: South Carolina does not require a driver to sign a traffic ticket, but in another state refusing to sign may lead to arrest under that state's laws.

cards.front: When may an officer search your vehicle without a warrant?
cards.back: If an officer believes a crime has been committed, the officer may search your vehicle without a court-issued warrant as long as there is probable cause.

cards.front: Why should you never flee from law enforcement?
cards.back: Never try to flee from law enforcement, since police chases cause many deadly collisions and the penalties for fleeing are worse than any original traffic citation.

cards.front: How do you report an officer you believe acted inappropriately?
cards.back: If you believe an officer acted inappropriately, report it to the officer's agency promptly; the officer's name and agency appear on the ticket, or you may ask for them.

cards.front: How should you behave if others with you are arrested?
cards.back: Do not make threatening motions or statements, keep your emotions in check, never interfere with the arrest of others with you and never resist arrest.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: large vehicle no zones and turns, emergency vehicles, law enforcement stops, the move-over law and slow-moving vehicles

cards.front: Where should you especially watch for slow-moving vehicles?
cards.back: Watch for slow-moving vehicles, especially in rural areas.

cards.front: What does an orange and red triangle on a vehicle's back mean?
cards.back: A fluorescent or reflective orange and red triangle on the back of a farm, construction or animal-drawn vehicle means it travels at less than twenty-five miles per hour, so approach with care and pass only when it is safe.

cards.front: Why pass farm equipment with caution?
cards.back: Tractors, combines and other farm equipment cross roads and travel on rural state highways, and their operators most likely cannot hear approaching vehicles over the machinery noise, so pass with caution.

cards.front: What rights do horseback riders and animal-drawn vehicles have on the road?
cards.back: Animal-drawn vehicles and horseback riders have the same right to use the road as motor vehicles, must follow the same rules and can suffer heavy damage and injury if hit.

cards.front: How should you pass an animal-drawn vehicle or rider?
cards.back: Pass animal-drawn vehicles and riders with caution, do not honk or rev your engine, which may scare the animal, and expect them to make left turns into fields and driveways.

cards.front: How do farm machinery and animals differ as hazards when you pass?
cards.back: Farm machinery operators may not hear you coming, while animals pulling a vehicle or carrying a rider may be frightened by a horn or a revving engine.

recaps.module: Stopping, passing and following large vehicles

recap_hooks.text: Large vehicles take longer to stop, so never cut in front of one, and move back in only when its whole front shows in your rearview mirror.
Do not follow a large vehicle too closely, and stay where its driver can see you in the side mirrors.
Trucks may swing wide to turn right, so never slip between a turning truck and the curb, and always stop behind the stop line.

recaps.module: Emergency vehicles and the move-over law

recap_hooks.text: Pull to the edge for a moving emergency vehicle, and for a stopped one slow down and change lanes away from it when safe.
When an officer stops you, pull over safely, turn off the engine, turn on your flashers, stay inside and keep your hands on the wheel.
Accepting a ticket is not an admission of guilt, and you contest it in court, never at the roadside.
An orange and red triangle marks a slow vehicle, and you should pass farm equipment and animals with caution and without honking.
